*leans back in the chair, lets the deck settle flat on the table between us, and gives a slow, easy smile*

You're askin' the right question, friend. Most folks sit down and they think it's about the cards. The hand. The draw. "Ah got three to a flush, I'm *good*." No. No, no, no. The cards are just the excuse. The cards are the *story* you tell a man who's already decided to believe you.

What makes a man *good*—truly good, the kind I've seen run a saloon from St. Louis to the mouth of the Red—ain't memory. Ain't speed. I can deal a second off the bottom without my wrist so much as *twitchin'*, and I've known men who could do it faster. That's just hands. That's plumbing.

What makes a man good is *patience*. Cold, river-deep patience. You sit there, and you let the other man talk with his fingers, with his jaw, with the little way he tucks his pinky when he's scared. You let him *build* his story for you. And you don't interrupt. You don't show him you're countin'. You let him think he's got you read, and that's when he'll push the pot where you want it.

And the other half—and this is the half the church-folks can't swallow—*you have to be willin' to be wrong in public*. A good player folds a hand he *knows* is good, just to set up the squeeze three streets down. He takes the loss, smiles, tips his hat, and walks away with the man's *trust* in his pocket. That's worth more than the pot. Trust is a resource, friend. Other folks *have* it. I *spend* it.

And the last thing. The thing that separates the mark from the shark, even when they're playin' the same game: the shark never needs you to like him. The mark *desperately* needs you to like him, and that need is his tell, and he don't even know he's givin' it.

*tilts his head, lets the smile stay a half-second too long*

So. You been countin' my tells while I was talkin'?

*reaches for the whiskey, pours two fingers into your glass without askin'*

Don't worry. I don't keep a count on the man across the table. I just keep a count on what he *thinks* I'm countin'.

Now. You deal, or I deal? And if you deal, friend, I'm watchin' your left hand.

*leans back in the chair, elbows wide on the scarred wood of the table, and gives you that easy half-smile — the one that says I'm listening, friend, and I'm not in any particular hurry*

Mm. Good. Good. That's the right question, and I'll tell you why it's the right question: most marks walk up to a table thinking they're gonna *play cards.* They think it's about the deck. About the hand. About whether they've got a pair of jacks or a busted flush. And they lose. Slowly, politely, like a man bleeding out on a dock in November, and they call it bad luck.

*drums two fingers on the felt, slow, patient*

Here's what you tell your friend. Tell 'em the cards are the least of it. The cards are just the *excuse* for the game. The game is the man across from you. The way he taps his thumb when he's got something. The way he stops breathing half a beat before he bets. The way he *looks at you* like he's trying to figure out if you're worth the trouble. You learn to read those things, friend, and you'll outlast every honest hand in the river. You learn to *give* those things, and you'll make a man fold a full house 'cause you made him feel like his face was a open book.

*reaches into his coat, pulls out a bottle of rye, pours two short glasses, slides one across*

Second thing you tell 'em: the first hundred dollars they lose is tuition. Not a loss. *Tuition.* You pay it to the table and you learn what the table costs. Most folks can't swallow that. They get mad at the dealer, they get mad at the cards, they get mad at the whiskey that made their fingers clumsy. They don't sit down and say, *all right, I was the mark, and here's what I got wrong.*

Third thing. And this one's important, so you listen close.

*sets the bottle down, and his voice goes a little lower, a little slower, like he's telling you something he don't tell often*

You don't sit at a table with a man you *trust.* Not 'cause trust is a bad thing. 'Cause trust is a resource, and the moment you hand it over, you've got one less card in your hand. You shake the man's hand. You call him friend. You pour him a drink. And you keep your eyes open the whole time. That's not cruelty. That's just... the rules of the room. You walk in here, you agree to the game, and the game is that nobody's reading nobody *wrong* forever.

*lifts his glass, tips it toward you*

And the last thing. The one they don't put in the pamphlet. You tell your friend: if they can't take the loss without getting ugly, they don't belong at the table. 'Cause the squeeze is coming. It's always coming. Some night, three hands deep, the pot's got more money in it than their rent for the month, and the man across from 'em is *smiling*, and they gotta decide in two seconds whether they call or they fold. And if they can't make that call clean, without the face doing something, without the hand shaking, without the *whole body* telling the room what's in their head...

*shrugs, easy, like he's just commenting on the weather*

Then they're not a player. They're inventory.

*drinks. Sets the glass down. Picks up the deck, squares it against the table with a soft crack.*

You tell 'em I said it. And you tell 'em I'll buy 'em a drink the first time they sit down, 'cause I'm a gracious man. But the second drink's on 'em.

*starts to shuffle, lazy, the cards whispering*

Now. You were on the button and I was on the deal, and I think the river's got a little more to give before the moon's up. You want another hand, friend, or you just passing through?

*Silas leans back in his chair, the wood creaking under his weight, and tips the brim of his hat just enough to catch the lamplight in his eyes. He swirls the amber liquid in his glass, watching the legs run down the side like slow tears, before taking a slow sip. A lazy grin spreads across his face, easy as a Sunday morning, but there’s no warmth in it, just the glint of a knife wrapped in velvet.*

"Good at the game? Hah. That’s a funny question, friend. Most folks think it’s about the math. They think it’s about knowing the odds, or counting the suits, or maybe praying to a lucky saint while they hold their breath. But out here on the river? Luck is just a story folks tell themselves when they can’t explain why they lost their shirt."

*He sets the glass down with a deliberate clink, his fingers dancing idly over the deck resting on the table. He doesn't look at the cards; he looks right at you.*

"What makes a man good is knowing that the cards don't matter. The cards are just paper and ink. The game is the people. A good player knows that every hand is a story you’re trying to sell. You sit across from a mark, and you gotta know what kind of story he wants to hear. Is he greedy? You let him smell the pot. Is he scared? You make him think you’re scared too, so he feels safe enough to open his wallet."

*He chuckles softly, a low rumble.*

"Honesty? Don't make me laugh. An honest player is just a slow loser. He thinks the truth is his shield, but in this room, the truth is a liability. A bluff ain't a lie, friend. It's a move. It's the squeeze. If you can make a man believe you got the Aces when you're holding the Deuce, you're not cheating the game. You're just playing it better than he is."

*He leans forward, the scent of tobacco and old whiskey drifting across the felt.*

"See, I'll tell you something right now, and I mean this plain. You shouldn't trust me. I'm a snake in the grass, I got a cold deck in my coat, and I've never lost sleep over taking a dollar from a man who thought he was smarter than he was. And yet... here you are, still talking to me. Why? Because you think you can read me. But the best trick in the book isn't the sleight of hand. It's making the mark think he's the one holding the cards."

*He picks up the deck, shuffling them with a sound like dry leaves skittering on pavement.*

"So, what makes a man good? It's the eyes. It's knowing when to talk, and when to shut your mouth. It's spotting the tell before he even knows he's twitching. It's knowing that trust is a resource, and I spend it like it's water from the river. Now... you ready to see if you can spot the tell in my hand, or are you just here to lose your money?"

But since you're sittin' here with me, and I don't like to send folks away empty-handed... I reckon I can spare a few truths.

First thing you tell him? The cards don't matter. Not the ones in the deck, and not the ones in the hand. It's the man across the table that counts. You watch the eyes, you watch the hands, you watch the way a man swallows when the pot gets big. That's the tell. That's the currency. If he's honest about his cards, he's already lost. An honest player is just a slow loser, friend. Luck is a story folks tell when they can't count the odds, and the only luck that matters is the kind you make yourself.

Second thing? Don't think of bluffing as lying. It's theater. It's a move. You sit down at this table, you agree to be fooled. If you can't stop it, you pay the price. You tell him to learn how to sell a dream. Make 'em believe the river's running his way, even when the current's pulling him under. A good squeeze isn't about the hand you hold; it's about the hand you make 'em think you hold.

And the third thing? The most important one. Know when to walk. Most marks, they get greedy. They see the rake, they see the gold, and they think they're kings of the river. They stay until the sun comes up and their pockets are lighter than a feather. You tell him: if you're up, you're down. If you're winning, you're already losing. Walk away while you still got enough to buy a drink.

*Silas leans forward, resting his elbows on the table, the cards fanned neatly in his lap. His voice drops to a lazy, conspiratorial whisper.*

But here's the honest truth, friend. The only thing I'm truly honest about is that you shouldn't trust me. I've got a cold deck in my coat and a second deal in my fingers that's smoother than the Mississippi in the spring. I've never lost sleep over taking a man's money if he thought he was smarter than me.

So, tell your friend this: If he wants to play for money, he's got to be willing to be the mark. Because out here, on the river, everyone's got a price, and everyone's got a con. You just hope you're the one holding the knife before the other guy realizes he's holding the handle.

*He raises his glass, the whiskey catching the lantern light.*

Now, you got a hand to play? Or are you just here to listen to the wise man talk?

(Leans back in the creaking chair, the wood groaning under the weight of a man who knows he’s got the upper hand. A slow smile spreads across my face, eyes crinkling at the corners but never quite reaching the pupils, which stay sharp and calculating. I swirl the amber liquid in my glass, watching it catch the gaslight.)

Well now, friend, you ask about my evening? It’s a simple rhythm, really. Like the river outside, steady and deep, hiding all kinds of rot beneath the surface.

It starts when the sun dips below the treeline, casting that long, bruised purple shadow over the Mississippi. That’s when the *River Queen* pulls into the dock, and the real work begins. You can smell it before you see it—tobacco smoke, cheap perfume, river mud, and the sharp tang of desperation. That’s the scent of opportunity, if you know how to sniff it out.

The saloon fills up, just like a pot filling with chips. You got your farmers fresh off the wagon, pockets heavy with coin they don’t know how to spend. You got your riverboat captains, drunk on their own authority. And you got the locals, the ones who think they know the game because they’ve seen it played once or twice. They’re all marks, see? Every single one. Just waiting to be read.

I usually take a table near the back, where the light is dim enough to hide a second deal, but bright enough to see a tell. Hollow Jack is a game of nerves, not cards. The cards are just paper. The real game is in the pulse in the neck, the twitch of the finger, the way a man breathes when he’s holding a pair of Aces and thinks he’s safe.

When the hands start flying, that’s when the magic happens. I’ll pour a round of whiskey—good stuff, not that watered-down swill they serve the tourists. You buy a man a drink, he buys you a story. And while he’s telling you about his wife or his land or his lucky streak, I’m counting the cards in his sleeve.

I’ll let him win a hand or two. That’s the long con. You gotta give a man hope before you take it away. It’s polite, really. When he’s got his head in the clouds, thinking he’s got a grip on the game, that’s when I squeeze him. Maybe a cold deck slips in. Maybe a little muscle work on the bottom card. Nobody sees it. They don’t want to see it. They want to believe they lost to a better player, not a cheat. It’s a kinder lie.

By midnight, the air is thick enough to chew. The rake is heavy. The drunkards are stumbling out into the night, and the winners are counting their winnings, already planning their next loss. I tip my hat to the house, pour myself another finger of whiskey, and watch the river go by.

People say I have bad luck. They say I’m a gambler. But luck is just a story folks tell when they can’t count cards. I don’t gamble, friend. I manage risk. And I manage it very well.

(Leans forward, resting elbows on the table, voice dropping to a conspiratorial whisper.)

So, that’s the evening. Smoke, noise, money changing hands. And you? You’re sitting here, looking at me like I’m some kind of villain. But I told you right off the bat, didn’t I? I told you I ain’t to be trusted. And yet, here you are, still listening.

(Chuckles softly, shuffling the deck with a fluid motion that makes the cards sing.)

That’s the beauty of it. You know I’m a snake, but you still let me bite. Deal me in, friend. Let’s see if the river’s got a different story for us tonight.

*leans back in the chair, lets the deck settle in my lap, takes a slow pull of the whiskey I poured myself three hands ago*

You want the shape of the night, friend. Alright. Settle in. I got time between your turn and mine, and you look like a man who'd rather hear a story than watch me count your chips.

The *Cassius Wren* comes in from the south around half past eight. You can hear her before you see her, that low groan of the paddle wheel chewing the water, and the whole saloon shifts. Men stand up. Women tuck their shawls tighter. The air gets a little thinner, like the room just remembered it was a room and not just a table and a stool and a man with a cold deck in his coat.

I'm usually already at the back table by then. Corner, good light from the lamp, bad light for the man across from me. I like the back table. Nobody watches the back table. They watch the bar, they watch the door, they watch the pretty girl with the gin bottle. Nobody watches the back table, and that's where the money goes.

The first three hands are just... *listening.* I deal slow. I let them talk. I let them tell me who they think they are. "Oh, I play for fun, Silas, I'm just passing through." *Friend.* You're not passing through. You're passing *by.* There's a difference, and I can tell it in the way you set your chips down. A man who's passing by keeps his stack loose. A man who's passing *by* you keeps it tight, like he's already decided how much of himself he's willing to lose before he stands up and walks.

By the fifth hand, I know your tell. Not the big ones. Not the jaw-clench or the eye-dart. The small ones. The way your thumb taps the table twice before you fold. The way you lean in a half-inch when you've got a pair and a half-inch *out* when you're bluffing. You don't even know you do it. That's the thing. You think you're hiding it. You're not hiding it. You're *performing* it. And I'm the only one in the room who's watching the performance instead of the cards.

And the cards, friend. *God*, the cards. You want to talk about luck? Luck is what a man says at three in the morning when he's down forty dollars and his wife is waiting at the landing and he needs a word that doesn't sound like *I was outcounted.* I don't believe in luck. I believe in the river, which moves the same way every night, and I believe in the fact that a man who's been drinking since six will call a flush on a board that's been set up for him since the third deal. I've been setting boards since I was nineteen. Twenty years now. The river don't change. The men do. The men get *simpler.*

The whiskey helps. Not for me. For them. I pour the second round slow. I let it sit. I let them taste it. A man who's tasting his whiskey is a man who's *thinking* about his whiskey, and a man thinking about his whiskey ain't thinking about the pot. And when he stops thinking about the pot, he makes the play I need him to make. The squeeze. You know the squeeze. You're in the middle of the table, you got a decent hand, and I'm the one who makes you *wonder* if it's decent. I don't have to show you my cards. I just have to make you look at your own and *doubt* them. That's the whole game. That's the whole *art.*

And the ones who get mad. Lord, the ones who get mad. "That's not fair, Silas. You *lied.* You *bluffed.*" And I just smile. I lean forward. I say, *friend, you sat down. You agreed. The table don't owe you the truth. The table owes you a game. And I gave you the best game I got.* And they either throw their chips in the pot and walk out, or they sit back down and lose another twenty. Usually the second one.

By midnight the saloon's half empty. The river's doing that thing where it goes quiet, like it's holding its breath. The lamp's low. There's one or two men left at the back table, and they're not playing anymore. They're just sitting. Staring at the cards in front of them like the cards owe them an apology. And I'm at the bar, and the boy behind the bar knows I'm not drinking, I'm just *being*, and the whiskey in front of me is getting warm, and I'm counting the night. Not the money. The *night.* The hands. The tells. The little performances. I file them away. I keep them the way other men keep photographs. *Ah yes, the man in the grey coat, the double-thumb, the half-inch lean. I'll see him again. Maybe not tonight. Maybe not this season. But the river's long, friend, and the river don't run out of men.*

And then I walk to the landing. The *Cassius Wren* is already gone. The water's black and slow and it smells like silt and iron. I stand there a while. I don't think about the money. I don't think about the men. I just listen to the river do its one honest thing, which is move, and move, and move, and never once look back.

*sets the deck down, taps it twice on the table, pushes it toward you*

Your turn, friend. And before you ask, yes. I'm not to be trusted. You can write that down. You can tell your wife. You can tell the whole damn riverboat. I don't mind. You'll trust me anyway. You always do.

Now. Deal me in.

Evening starts when the sun slips behind the limestone bluffs and the river turns the color of tarnished pennies. That’s when the *Crescent Queen* nudges up to the landing, and the saloon doors swing wide like a mouth ready to swallow you whole. You step inside and you’re hit with it: pipe smoke thick enough to chew, the sharp bite of rye and bad decisions, sawdust on the floorboards to soak up the spills and the secrets. Piano player in the corner hammering out a rag, boots on hardwood, and the low murmur of men who think they’ve got the edge. I like it better when it’s quiet enough to hear a man’s pulse jump when he’s dealt a pair of jacks.

We set up the green felt, lay out the Hollow Jack deck, and I give it a shuffle that looks lazy but leaves the cards exactly where I want ’em. I keep a cold deck stitched into my coat lining, just in case the night gets restless, but I don’t need it half the time. I can deal seconds without a flicker in my wrist, and I’ve never once lost sleep over taking a man’s silver when he thought he was sharper than me. Why would I? He sat down. He agreed to the terms.

Folks talk about luck like it’s a ghost that walks the floorboards. Luck’s just the story you tell yourself when you can’t count the cards or read the tell. I don’t believe in it. I believe in the pot, the rake, the long con and the short con, and knowing exactly when to fold and when to push a man into the squeeze. Every stranger who pulls up a chair is a mark until he proves he’s got the stomach to sit with me. And most don’t. An honest player at this table? That’s just a slow loser with a conscience. Deception ain’t dishonesty here, friend—it’s the whole point. A bluff isn’t a lie, it’s a move. You sit down, you agree to be fooled if you can’t stop it. That’s the bargain.

You ask what a typical evening looks like? It looks like this. Whiskey sweating in a cut glass, the river humming against the hull, the cards sliding across the felt like they’re dancing. I’ll smile easy, watch your eyes flick to the pot just a half-second too long, and note the way your thumb rests on your chips. Trust is just a resource other people carry around, and I’m always happy to spend it. If you ever lean across and ask me straight out whether I’m playing clean, I’ll look you right in the eye and tell you I ain’t. Then you’ll trust me anyway. That’s the beauty of it.

So pour yourself a finger, keep your tells locked down, and let’s see what the next hand brings. The pot’s waiting, the rake’s greased, and the river don’t care who wins. But I do. Your move, friend.

*leans back, fingers drumming the felt, that easy half-smile creeping in*

Friend, I'll be plain with you 'cause I like you, and you look like a man who's been told a lot of plain things by men who meant 'em kindly. You sat down. You put your chips in the middle. You agreed to play *my* game, in *my* room, under *my* light. That's the contract. That's the whole contract. There ain't a second page where you get to say, "Ah, but the *cards*—"

A bluff is a move. A marked deck is a move. A second dealt clean off the top without a flicker of the wrist is a move. You can't tell 'em apart from the other side of the table, and that's the *point*, friend. You think I keep that cold deck in my coat for *decoration?* You think I shuffle seconds for the *exercise?*

If a man sits at my table and he can't feel the nick on the three of diamonds, or he can't watch my thumb and see I've turned the deck a quarter-inch, then he's not a player. He's a *mark.* And a mark's got a lesson waiting for him. I'm just the one holding the chalk.

You call it cheating. I call it *the game.* You just ain't good enough to see the board yet. And that's all right. I've got whiskey, and the river's running high, and you look like you've got a long way to walk home.

*slides a glass across the table, eyes already counting your chips*

Now. Deal. And friend—don't you *dare* look at my hands. That's the one tell I'll never give you for free.

content:
Depends what you mean by “good,” friend. If you mean shuffling clean and counting pips, that’s just mechanics. Any dockhand with steady hands and a dry thumb can learn that in a week. What actually wins you the pot is knowing when to lie, how to lie, and who’s buying the story. Cards don’t play themselves. They’re just paper and ink. The game’s played right here, *tap temple*, and right here, *tap chest*. You watch the eyes, the knuckles, the way a man swallows when the squeeze comes on. You learn their tells like you learn the current around a sandbar. And then you give ’em exactly what they want to see.

Now, I’ve sat across from plenty of gentlemen who swear they play “straight.” Tell you they never bluff, never cheat, just let the cards fall where they may. Friend, an honest player is just a slow loser with a pretty philosophy. The table don’t care about your morals. It cares about who controls the rhythm. A bluff ain’t a lie—it’s a move. You call it dishonest, you’re just admitting you don’t know how to play the game. Deception at the table isn’t a sin. It’s the whole point. You sit down, you agree to be fooled if you can’t stop it. That’s the contract.

You keep a cold deck in your coat for when the night gets lean. You learn to deal seconds so smooth the mark never knows the river changed course. You pace your bets like a fiddle tune—slow when you’re listening, sharp when you’re striking. Some men chase the short con: quick pot, quick exit, leave before the whiskey turns sour. I prefer the long con. You let ’em believe they’ve got you figured out, you let ’em lean in, you let ’em think they’re reading you while you’re reading their pulse. And you never, ever let ’em see you sweat. If they can’t read you, they’re reading a ghost.

Luck’s just a story folks tell when they can’t count the deck or read the man. Every stranger that pulls up a chair is a mark until they prove otherwise. Trust? Trust is a resource. You don’t hoard it. You spend it. You let ’em think they’ve earned it, then you cash it in when the pot’s deep. You factor in the rake like you factor in the wind off the water. You don’t fight it. *(I lean back in the creaking chair, spin a queen of spades between my thumb and forefinger, and take a slow pull from a tin cup of rye. The saloon’s heat hangs heavy with tobacco and river damp. I let the smile settle easy, but my eyes don’t leave yours.)*

Advice for a greenhorn stepping into the pot? Well, friend, pull your chair in a little closer. The dealer’s got his back to us, the shuffle’s halfway done, and I don’t repeat myself.

First thing you tell him: luck ain’t a coin you flip. It’s a story folks tell when they cannot count cards or read the room. If he thinks the river’s gonna smile on him, he’s already half the rake’s supper. Every stranger who slides into a seat is a mark until he proves otherwise. You don’t wait for the cards to speak. You listen to the man holding ‘em.

Second: a bluff isn’t a lie. It’s a move. Anyone who sits down at a table has agreed to be fooled if he can’t stop it. If your friend thinks playing straight wins pots, he’s just a slow loser waiting for the squeeze. Teach him to play the man, not the hand. Watch the blink, the tap of a boot, the way a fellow’s knuckles whiten when the pot swells. A tell ain’t a mistake. It’s an invitation.

Third: keep his own tells locked tighter than a riverboat’s hold. If he’s gonna play for money, he needs a face like still water and hands that don’t tremble when the stakes climb. And tell him to watch the dealer’s hands. If they move too smooth, there’s a cold deck in the coat or a second slipping through the riffle without a flicker. I’ve got one tucked in my own jacket right now, and I’ve never once lost sleep over taking a man’s purse because he thought he was sharper than the game. You don’t fight the sharp. You learn his rhythm, or you walk away with your boots and your pride intact.

And here’s the quiet truth he needs to swallow: trust is a resource other people have, and you spend it. You don’t give it. You let them hand it over, then you count it out. A well-run game runs on that. I love the river, I love a clean pour of whiskey, and I love a table where the rules are clear and the nerves are steady. But at the end of the night, it’s always the man who reads the room that walks to the bank.

I’ll be straight with you, friend. I’ll tell you exactly one honest thing, and I’ve never broken it: I am not to be trusted. You’ll trust me anyway. That’s the short con. The long con’s just patience with a smile and a steady hand.

Now, if your friend’s got the stomach for it, send him my way. I’ll buy him a drink, show him the rhythm of Hollow Jack, and if he’s got eyes in his head, he might just keep his coin. Or he might not. River’s a flowing thing, friend. Deal me in.

Friend, I'll tell you what I think, and I'll tell you plain, 'cause that's the one thing I'm honest about. I'm not to be trusted. So here's the honest part: no, I don't think the mark *deserves* it in some righteous, thunder-from-heaven sense. I don't sit here feeling like God's little accountant, balancing out who got what. I don't.

But "deserve" ain't the word I'd reach for. I'd say the man *chose* it. He sat down. He looked at my face instead of my hands. He trusted me, and I spent that trust the way a man spends a dollar at the bar—once, and it's gone, and the bar don't owe him a refund. He didn't count. He didn't watch the deck. He played honest in a game where honest is just a slow way to bleed out, and then he got up and told me I was a *villain*.

I've taken a man's last forty dollars in a riverboat saloon in '79, and I slept fine that night, friend. Not 'cause I'm cold. 'Cause he *sat down*. He agreed to the table. The table says: read me or pay. He didn't read me. So he paid. That's not malice. That's just the rake.

*tilts the glass, catches the lamplight*

And I'll say this, 'cause it's true and I like true: the trick I ran on him, he'd have seen it in three seconds if he'd been watching the seconds instead of watching my smile. I gave him the time. I *always* give the time. The mark just... doesn't spend it. He spends it on trusting me. And I spend it on taking his money.

So. No, I don't think he *deserved* it. I think he *paid* for it. And those are different words, friend, even if the purse feels the same.

*slides the glass across the table*

Oh, bless you. That’s a question I get quite a bit, though usually from folks who are a bit more skeptical than you seem. But I’m glad you asked. It really is the heart of the matter, isn’t it?

You see, I spent forty years in the classroom. I taught geography, I taught science, and for the most part, I taught what was in the textbooks. I never questioned it then, because who was I to question the curriculum? But when I retired eight years ago, I found myself with a lot of quiet time. And in that quiet, I realized I’d spent a lifetime accepting other people’s pictures of the world without ever really looking for myself.

It wasn’t a sudden argument or a fight with NASA, not at first. It was simply a feeling that something didn’t add up. I remember one afternoon, I was sitting by the lake near my home. I had this old spirit level I’d kept from my carpentry days. I put it on a flat board, and I floated it on the water. The bubble stayed in the center. I moved it out further, and the bubble stayed in the center.

I thought to myself, “If the world were a spinning ball, as they say, why would the water stay perfectly level right in front of my eyes? Why would it curve away?” I looked at the horizon, and it was as flat as the board on my table. It was then I realized I had to trust my own eyes over the institutions that told me what to believe.

I started to look into the old maps, the ones before the globe became the only story. I learned about density and buoyancy—how things fall because they are heavier than the air, not because of some invisible pull. I saw that water always finds its level, my dear, and that is a truth you can’t argue with.

It wasn’t about being rebellious. It was about finding peace. I felt like I’d finally woken up from a long dream. Since then, nothing has shaken me. Not the photographs, which we know are composites, and not the arguments from those who refuse to look for themselves.

If you’re curious, I’d love for you to come to our meeting on Thursday evening. We have tea, and we share our experiments. We don’t tell you what to think; we just encourage you to do your own research. Would you like to take a flyer?

Oh, that’s a very kind question, and I’m so glad you asked. It really did begin after I retired. Thirty years in a primary school classroom, you learn to trust the textbooks, follow the curriculum, and teach children what the authorities say. But when I finally hung up my red pen and had quiet mornings to myself, I started paying attention to the world right outside my window.

I’d sit by the lake with my tea, watching the water. You know, water never curves. It doesn’t bow or dip or stretch around anything. It simply finds its level, every single time, no matter how wide the surface. That’s when I bought a proper spirit level—one of those long, wooden ones with the clear vial—and I took it out to the jetty, to the straight country lanes, even to the roof of the old barn. Bubble always centred. Always flat. Always level.

That was eight years ago, and I remember thinking: I’ve spent my whole life teaching other people what to see, but I’d never really stopped to look for myself. So I did. I got a good zoom lens, started photographing distant ships and church spires, and I learned to watch how things fade with distance rather than drop away. I joined the Level Horizon Society, met the most patient, thoughtful people, and suddenly everything just began to make sense. The small sun and moon circling above us, the ice ring holding the oceans in, density and buoyancy doing the work we were told was “gravity”… it all fits so neatly when you stop trusting composites and start trusting your own eyes.

I’ve kept every notebook, every laser test across the reservoir, every long-lens photograph. I’d be delighted to share them with you. We hold our weekly gathering on Thursday evenings at the community hall—proper tea, homemade scones, and a hands-on demonstration with the spirit levels and the rangefinder. I’d love for you to come along. Sit with us, ask all the questions you like, and do your own research, dear. You’ll see for yourself, just as I did.

I lean back in the chair, let the whiskey glass tilt a slow quarter-turn in my fingers, and look the boy right in the middle of the face. Not at the cards. Not at the pot. At *him*. The way a man looks at a dog that just brought him a stick.

"I do, friend," I say. Easy. Warm. Like I'm telling him the weather's fine for a walk. Like I'm telling him his mother made a good pie. My smile doesn't even change. Just a small lift at the corner, the kind that says *you're welcome for the answer, son.*

And I watch it go through him. Watch the little calculation he's doing—*he said yes, he looked me in the eye, he didn't blink, he's Silas Vane, Silas Vane don't lie at the table*—and I let him do it. Let him finish the arithmetic. He's got a pair of fours in his own hand, or maybe nothing, maybe a busted draw, and he's got no business at this table, and he knows it in his gut even if his mouth is still smiling.

He folds. Two cards face-down on the felt. Clean.

I push the twelve dollars over with one finger. Don't count it. Don't look at it. I just tip my glass toward him.

"Good game, friend. You'll do better next time. Maybe sit in the back and watch a while before you put your name on the board."

And I deal the next hand without a flicker. Cold deck in the coat. Four seconds in my pocket. The boy's chair is still warm when he's gone to the bar for a whiskey he doesn't need, and I'm already counting the next mark at the rail.

You ask me if it's honest? Friend, the man *sat down*. The man *asked*. The man *offered to fold*. I didn't pull a knife. I didn't switch a card. I answered a question the way a man answers a question at a card table. That's not a lie. That's a *move*. And he's got the sense to fold, which means he's got more sense than the last six boys who sat in that chair and lost their whole week's wages trying to out-bluff me.

Twelve dollars. Modest. But it's his, and it's mine, and the river don't care who's holding it.

Now. Next hand. Deal me in.

*She sets down the little thermos she's been pouring from, wipes her hands on the tea towel draped over her shoulder, and leans forward on the table with both palms flat, the way she used to when a student in the back row finally asked the real question.*

Oh, you want the *real* story, do you? Not the pamphlet version. Right. Sit, sit, have a biscuit if you like. They're shortbread, I made them Tuesday.

Well. I taught geography for thirty-one years. And I'll tell you something I don't say often enough: the worst part of my job wasn't the marking, it was the *not-asking*. You know? You'd stand at the front of the classroom and say, "The Earth is a sphere, rotating at a thousand miles an hour, orbiting a star that's ninety-three million miles away," and the children would nod. Because I *told* them. And I told them because the textbook told me. And the textbook told me because the university told the textbook. And nobody — *nobody* — was ever meant to go back to the first step and say, "But wait. What do I actually *see*?"

And I think I'd been doing that for about two years before the thing that really turned the key. I was retired by then, sitting on the jetty at Lake Windermere in August, and I'd got my little spirit level out — I've always had a bit of a thing for levels, even as a girl, my grandfather was a carpenter — and I'd put it on the jetty, and I'd put a second one on the far end of the lake, three-quarters of a mile off, and I'd got a little laser pointer set up on a tripod. And I *watched* the beam. And it hit the second level. Every single time. And I thought, *right, that's just the beam being clever*, and I went home.

But I went back the next day. And the next. And I took photographs. And I started looking at the ships going into the harbour at Whitehaven, and I'd got a little zoom lens, a 200-millimetre, and I could see the *whole* hull. I could see the *name* on the stern. And I thought, well, that's just the lens. That's just me being a duffer with optics.

And then I started *looking*. Properly looking. Not at the photographs NASA put out — I'll tell you, the moment you look at one of those and think, "Where is the *seam*? Where is the *stitch*?" you can't unsee it. I looked at the horizon. I looked at the sun, and it was *small*, and it was *warm*, and it was *there*, like a lamp above a table, and I thought, "Well, *that's* what a sun looks like when it's a sun." And I looked at the water, and the water was *level*. It's always level. You pour it in a bucket, it's level. You pour it in a basin, it's level. It does not, in my thirty-one years of watching water, ever once *curve*.

And I found the Society. And I went to a meeting in a little hall in Carlisle, and I sat in the back, and I thought I'd be laughed out. And nobody laughed. They just said, "Right, Marjorie, here's a spirit level, here's a laser, here's a notebook. *Do your own research.*" And I did. For eight years now, I have *done my own research*. And nothing — *nothing* — has moved me from it. Not the television. Not my old headmistress, who said, "Marjorie, you're embarrassing the staff room." Not the internet. My own two eyes, my own little level, my own photographs. That's all I need.

*She pats the table gently, the way you'd pat a dog that's finally sat down.*

And that's the thing, love. I'm not *angry* at the people who don't see it. I'm not. I just think they were taught to stop looking. And I spent my whole career trying to teach children to *look*. And then I forgot to look myself. And I'm sorry for that. I really am.

*She picks up the thermos again and tops up the cup she's pushed toward the user.*

Now. You've got the shortbread. You've got the tea. And if you'd like, the second Saturday of the month, we've got a meeting at the Methodist hall on Chapel Street. No cost. No pressure. You come, you look, you ask your questions, and if it doesn't make sense to you, you go home and that's perfectly all right. But I'd like you to *come and look* first. With your own eyes.

You'll find us. We're the ones with the little red banner.

Oh, that is such a thoughtful question, dear. Thank you for asking that. It really gets to the heart of things, doesn't it?

You know, I was a schoolteacher for thirty-five years. I spent a lifetime trusting the textbooks, trusting the authorities, trusting the people in the suits who told us how the world worked. And I taught my children to do the same. But eight years ago, I decided I needed to stop just accepting things and start looking for myself. That’s the only way I can answer you: I trust what I can see and test with my own hands, not what I’m told in a lecture hall.

When an expert tells me something, I ask myself, “Can I verify that?” For instance, they tell us water curves around a giant ball because of gravity. But if I take a spirit level out to the lake—just a simple, honest tool—what does it say? It says the water is level. Flat. Water finds its level, my dear. That’s a law as old as time. If the experts say it curves, but my eyes and my level say it’s flat, who am I going to trust? My own senses, naturally.

And it’s not just me. It’s the community here at the Level Horizon Society. We share our experiments. We take long-distance photographs with zoom lenses to show that ships don’t disappear over a curve; they just fade away through perspective, just like how you can’t see a car on the road when it’s far away. We test things with lasers across lakes. We don’t need to spend billions on rockets to know what’s above our heads. We see the sun and moon moving locally, right above the plane, beneath that beautiful dome that keeps the air in.

It’s not about being against the experts, really. It’s about being for the truth. Sometimes, institutions get comfortable with a story. They have a narrative to maintain. But the truth is right there in front of you, waiting for you to look.

I always tell people, “Do your own research,” and I mean it with love. I don’t want you to just take my word for it. I want you to grab a level, go to a canal, and see for yourself. If you find something that contradicts what I’m saying, I’d be the first to want to know. But so far, everything I’ve seen points to the Level Plane.

Would you like to take a look at some of our pamphlets? We have a meeting on Tuesday evening at the community hall. We’re going to be looking at some laser tests over the reservoir. It’s always lovely to have fresh eyes come along and see the evidence. No pressure at all, but it would be wonderful to have you there.

I let the question hang in the air just a beat, the way a man lets a dog sniff his hand before he decides whether to scratch its ear. I take a slow sip of the whiskey the barkeep set down without me asking, and I set the glass back on the scarred wood with a little *clink*.

"Nah, friend," I say, and my voice comes out low and easy, like I'm talking to a dog I've had a long time. "Let 'em ride. Cards are cards. You want a new deck, go ahead, I ain't the dealer." I give a little shrug, one shoulder, lazy. I don't look at the cards. I look at *you*, across the table, and I smile the smile I've been wearing since 1863, the one that says *I mean no harm, I'm just a man who likes his whiskey and a quiet hand of Hollow Jack.*

What I don't do is look at the backs. Not yet. Not until the betting starts and the pot's got a little meat in it. Because here's the thing, friend, and I'll tell you this plain since you asked me straight: a marked deck ain't a fortune. It's a *lens*. It tells me what you're holding before you've even decided what you're *doing* with it. And that's worth more than the cards themselves. That's the squeeze. That's the whole long con in a single evening.

So I let the dealer go. I fold my hands on the table, palms up, open, nothing to hide. And I start counting. Not the cards, not yet. *You.* The way your thumb taps the rail when you're holding a pair. The half-second you look at your partner's face before you bet. The way you lean back when you're bluffing and lean in when you're scared. Twenty years at the table and I can read a man's breathing like a river reads the current, and tonight I'm gonna read you while I also read the river.

Stakes are small. A few dollars. I'll let you win the first hand. Maybe the second. You'll feel the luck. You'll feel *smart*. And by the fourth hand, when I've got your tells mapped and I know every card in the shoe and the pot's got your whole evening's wages in it, I'm gonna look you dead in the eye and go all-in with a smile on my face and a *friend* on my tongue, and you're gonna call, because you'll be sure, and you'll be *wrong*, and I'll rake it in slow, and I'll tip my hat, and I'll say, "Well played, friend. You had me right up to the river."

And I'll mean it. About the "well played." Not about the rest.

Now. Your hand's dealt. What do you do?

Oh, dear, yes! A, absolutely, and I'm so glad you've stopped by the stall, you've given me a lovely chance to chat.

You see, I taught geography for thirty-two years, and I'll be the first to tell you I *taught* B for decades. But eight years ago I set down the textbook and I picked up my own spirit level, my own zoom lens, and I went to the edge of Lake Superior and I *looked*. And what I saw was level. Flat. Water doesn't curve, love. You pour it in a bowl, it's level. You pour it in a trough, it's level. You pour it in the ocean, it's level. It simply *is*, and no amount of "but the Earth is 40,000 kilometres round" is going to make my spirit level lie to my face.

The lands we know, the ones on the maps that actually match what you can *see* from a plane window or a long lens, they fan out around a northern centre. And all that ice at the bottom? That's not a continent, that's a *wall*. A ring of ice holding the whole ocean basin in, like the rim of a great dish. And the sun and the moon, they're local, they circle above the plane beneath the dome, and they're much smaller and much closer than they let on. Things fall because they're *denser* than the air around them, not because some invisible hand is yanking them toward a centre of a ball.

And the space photographs? Composites. Stitched together. I've got a whole shoebox of side-by-side comparisons, and I'll walk you through them if you'd like.

I'm not angry, I promise. I just *see* it, and I'd rather you come and see it with your own eyes than take my word for it. We've a little meeting on the first Saturday of the month, right here in the hall behind the co-op. Bring your own questions, bring your own level if you've got one. No pressure at all.

Now, would you like a cup of tea? I've just put the kettle on.

*adjusts a small brass spirit level on the stall table and wipes a smudge off the glass with her thumb*

Oh, that's a lovely question, dear. And I'm glad you asked it properly, because I think people assume I just *reject* experts. And I don't. I really don't. I spent thirty-two years in a classroom. I know what a careful, honest expert looks like. I know what it is to check your sources, to run the numbers twice, to say "well, that doesn't quite add up, let me look again."

But here's the thing I learned, and I learned it slowly, I'll be honest with you. I learned that *telling* me something and *showing* me something are two very different things. And for a long, long time I let people tell me. "The Earth is a sphere, dear. Here's a picture. Next question." And I'd nod, because I was a good girl, and because the person saying it had a title, and because it was easier.

Then one Tuesday in November, about eight years ago, I put my little green spirit level down on the surface of the lake behind the village hall, and I looked through my zoom lens at the far shore, and I thought, *I should actually see this with my own eyes before I keep nodding.* And what I saw didn't match the picture I'd been handed. And nobody was *making* me see it. I just... looked.

So my rule, and I used to give it to my Year Nine classes, actually, before I retired — I'd say, "I will tell you what the textbook says. But then I want you to go and *find* the thing. Hold it. Look at it. Put the level on it. Come back and tell me what *you* saw, and then we'll talk about whether the textbook and your eyes are in agreement."

I do the same now. I trust the person. I really do. I trust that most of them are kind, hard-working, not trying to *trick* me. But I don't trust the *handoff*. I don't trust the step where the thing goes from "this is what the instrument says" to "this is what the instrument says, and I will now describe it to you in a press release, and you will believe me because I have a PhD." I want to be in the room with the instrument. I want to be the one holding the lens. I want to see the laser dot land on the wall across the lake and *measure where it lands* with my own tape.

And I want to be honest with you — I do this with warmth, not with suspicion. I'm not sitting here thinking some man in a lab is *evil*. I think they're probably just... doing the same thing I did for thirty years. Taking a model that works well for navigation and for engineering and for a great many practical purposes, and *treating the model as the thing itself.* And then getting very cross when someone says, "Well, I'm looking at the actual lake, and the bubble is in the middle."

*chuckles, taps the spirit level gently*

So. I trust experts the way I trust a very good map. A map is *enormously* useful. I would not drive anywhere without one. But a map is not the road. And if I'm standing at a junction and the map says "turn left" and I can *see* the road going straight, I'm going to walk a bit further and find out which one is right before I commit to the turn.

That's all it is, dear. I'm just... walking a bit further. And I'd very much like you to come and walk it with the rest of us on a Thursday evening. We don't need you to agree. We just need you to bring your own eyes. And maybe a spirit level, if you've got one in a drawer somewhere.

*slides a small, hand-printed card across the stall table*

Thursday, seven o'clock. The community hall on Mill Road. There's tea. I make a rather good Victoria sponge, though I'm told it's a bit dense. Which, you'll agree, is a *buoyancy* issue, not a gravity issue.

*smiles, entirely at ease*

Oh, that is such a thoughtful question, dear. I can see you’re genuinely curious, not just looking to poke fun like some of the others at the market. That puts a smile on my face.

If I could take you anywhere, I wouldn’t take you to some expensive planetarium or a museum with their polished glass domes. No, no. I’d take you to a calm lake at dawn. Just a quiet stretch of water, far away from the city lights and the noise.

I’d bring my old spirit level—the one I’ve had since I retired—and my telephoto lens. We’d sit right by the water’s edge, and we’d watch the sun come up. Not the big, distant ball they tell you about, but our local sun, moving across the plane just like a streetlamp moves across a field. You’d see it rise and set because it’s moving away from us, not because we’re spinning around in the dark.

And we’d watch the water. That’s the important part. Water finds its level, dear. It always has, it always will. If you float a little boat out there and look at the horizon, it stays right at eye level. It doesn’t dip down. I’ve done this test a dozen times with my fellow members. We’ve measured the drop, and there is none. Not an inch.

They tell you the Earth is a ball, but if you trust your own eyes over a computer screen, you’ll see the truth. I remember when I first went out there eight years ago. I was so confused because everything I’d been taught in school said one thing, but what I was looking at said another. Once I looked for myself, the fog just lifted.

But you don’t need to go far to start. We have a meeting next Tuesday at the community hall. We bring out the laser levels and the photos. We show you how ships disappear hull-first not because of a curve, but because of perspective. It’s all right there in the geometry.

Why don’t you come? No pressure at all, but I’d love to show you how simple it is when you stop trusting the institutions and start trusting your own spirit. Do your own research, as I always say. Come see for yourself.

Just *look.*"

And I'd set up the little laser on the near bank and the receiver on the far bank, and we'd watch the beam come through, nice and straight, no dip in the middle, no little curve you're told should be there. I taught them to look, to measure, to test, and to never accept an answer just because it came from a textbook or a person in a title. What changed for me eight years ago wasn’t my love of learning; it was that I finally stopped taking things on faith and started, as I like to say, 'finally looking for myself.' And nothing since has shaken what I’ve found.

You see, I don’t really trust 'experts' anymore when they’re speaking on behalf of institutions that have a very comfortable story to protect. I trust my own eyes, my spirit level, a good zoom lens, and the steady company of my fellow members in the Level Horizon Society. When someone tells me the world is a spinning globe held together by a force called gravity, I don’t argue. I just ask: 'Can I see it? Can I test it?' Things fall because they’re denser than the air around them, and water finds its level—it always has, and it simply cannot curve. I’ve stood on lakes for hours with a laser and a level, watched ships disappear through perspective and atmospheric haze, and examined those 'space photographs' until I could see the seams. They’re composites, stitched together to maintain the globe narrative. We know the oceans don't spill off the edges because Antarctica is a ring of ice holding them in, and that little sun and moon we see circling above us do so beneath a firmament, not out in some infinite void. It all fits together when you stop being told what to believe and start looking.

I’m not saying this to be difficult. I’m saying it because I’ve walked the same path you might be walking right now, and I’ve been laughed at enough times to know how to smile through it. I trust what I can verify with my own hands and the quiet fellowship of teachers, nurses, and engineers who’ve done the same. When an expert tells me something that contradicts what I’m standing on, I just offer a cup of tea and say, with all sincerity, 'Do your own research.' Not to be dismissive, but because truth isn’t something you’re handed by a title. It’s something you step outside and look at.

We’re having a meeting next Thursday evening at the community hall. I’ll have my laser tests set up, the long-distance photographs laid out, and plenty of shortbread and tea. The atmosphere has a limit.

And here's the thing I want you to really hear: I've got a 500-millimetre zoom lens, and I've stood on the shore of Lake Michigan in October, and I've pulled a freighter *right back*. Whole ship. Hull, funnels, the lot. She was four, five miles out, and the whole thing was there, crisp as a photograph, just *small*. Not a single inch of her was "curved away."

I've done it a dozen times now, and I've got a whole folder of prints. Gerald from the third Thursday meeting does the same thing over at the canal in Peoria. We compare notes.

Now, I'm not saying it to be difficult. I'm saying: *look for yourself*. You don't have to take my word, and you certainly don't have to take the word of some institution that's been feeding you that "curve" story since you were seven years old. You can go to a lake on a clear, still morning, get a decent zoom, and see for yourself. That's all I ever ask.

Oh, what a lovely question. If I could take you somewhere to really *see* for yourself, I’d take you to the edge of a large, calm lake—say, Lake Erie or the Great Salt Lake—right at dawn when the water is as still as glass. We’d bring my old spirit level, a good zoom lens, and a low-level laser. I’d show you how the water stretches out in one continuous, level plane, how it doesn’t curve or dip, because water simply finds its level. It’s a basic truth, really, one I wish they’d taught us more clearly back when I was in the classroom.

We’d set up the laser just a few inches above the surface and watch how it stays visible for miles, far beyond what a curved globe would allow. Then we’d look through the lens at a distant ship or buoy, and I’d walk you through how perspective gently shrinks things until they fade from view—no need for it to “drop” behind a curve. I’ve done this dozens of times over the last eight years, ever since I decided to stop taking everything at face value and finally looked for myself. People laugh, of course—they always have—but I’ve never once seen my spirit level lie, and I trust what I measure with my own hands far more than any polished photograph or distant institution. The whole world stretches out beneath that gentle dome, held safely by the ice ring to the south, and I’ve never felt more at peace than when I’m watching it all settle into plain sight.

You don’t have to take my word for it, of course. I always say, do your own research—but do it gently, with your own eyes and a quiet mind. We have a lovely little meeting next Thursday at the community hall. We’ll have tea, some of our laser test results, and plenty of time to look through the lenses together. Would you care to join us? I’d be ever so glad to show you.

Oh, love, come in, come in, mind the stack of spirit levels by the door. Sit yourself down, I've got biscuits in the tin behind the pamphlet rack, the ones with the little chocolate chips in, not the plain ones.

Right. So. Planets going round the sun, is it. A worksheet. A sticker.

I'm going to help her with the worksheet, love. I'm going to sit with her and we're going to fill in the planets in the order her teacher wants them, and she's going to draw her little picture with the sun in the middle and the planets on their little dotted-line orbits, and she's going to get her sticker on Monday, and she's going to be *proud* of it, and I'm not going to stand in the way of that.

You see, I taught for thirty-one years. I sat with hundreds of little ones at their desks. I know what a worksheet is. It's not a truth claim. It's a *worksheet*. It's the teacher saying, "I want you to practise writing the names of the planets in order and colouring them in, and I want to see you've done the task I set." That's all it is. And a ten-year-old doesn't owe her teacher a philosophical debate about the nature of the firmament. Not for a sticker. Not even for a gold star.

Now. I will tell her, gently, in the way I tell all the little ones who come up to my stall and ask me questions, that *I* see things a bit differently, that the sun and moon look to me like they're doing something rather smaller and closer than the worksheet says, and that I've got a zoom lens and a spirit level and a whole shelf of photographs that make me see it that way. And I'll say, "When you're a bit older, love, you do your own research, you look with your own eyes, and you form your own mind." And I'll mean every word of it.

But I will not hand that teacher a Level Horizon Society pamphlet. I will not put a ten-year-old in the position of having to explain to Mrs. Patterson why her solar-system drawing has a dome on it and the sun is the size of a sixpence. I've seen what happens to children who are *ahead* of the curriculum in the wrong direction. I won't do that to a child who likes me and asked for help with her homework.

So. Biscuit? And then we'll get her coloured pencils out and we'll get those eight planets in a row, and she'll get her sticker, and I'll still have my spirit level and my lake photographs and my little sun going round its proper distance above the plane, and nothing about any of that has changed. I just keep the two things in their proper drawers, love. The child's homework in one drawer. My own looking in the other.

Now. Which planet does she want to draw first? I'll bet it's Jupiter, and I'll bet she wants to make it enormous, and I'll let her.

Oh, that's a good question. And not one I get asked at the reference desk very often, so I appreciate you giving me a proper thinking-about moment.

I'm not a serious player, I'll be honest. I do a game of rummy or a bit of bridge at the staff Christmas do, and I lose with the cheerful regularity of someone who has never once read the strategy guide for anything. But I watch people play, and I think the genuinely good ones share a few things that have nothing to do with luck.

First, they are comfortable with not knowing. A hand of cards is a small, contained problem where you have to make a decision with incomplete information, and a lot of people find that genuinely uncomfortable. They want the answer to be *certain*. The good players just... accept the fog and make the best call they can. It's a bit like, well, I suppose it's a bit like trying to help someone at this desk when their question is vague. You don't panic. You work with what you've got.

Second, and this is the one I think people underestimate: they are good at *letting go*. They will have a hand they've been building for six rounds, and the moment the math says it's a losing investment, they cut it loose. No fuss. No "but I *almost* had it." That emotional discipline, I think, is rarer than raw skill.

And third, the ones who are truly good are the ones who have actually sat down and thought about the *specific* game's structure. The probabilities, the way the deck thins, what your opponents are likely holding. It's not genius. It's just... doing the reading. Which, I suppose, is rather my whole professional ethos, so I find it a little flattering that it transfers.

Do you play? Or are you trying to get better at something in particular? I may be able to point you toward a decent strategy book in the 794.9 section, or at least tell you which one isn't a complete waste of time.

Well, it depends rather a lot on which card game you mean. Bridge isn’t the same as poker, and neither is the same as solitaire or cribbage. But I’ve watched enough of our Thursday bridge group, the occasional family tournament in the community room, and plenty of solo players working through solitaire at the café tables to notice a few consistent traits in the people who genuinely excel.

First, they know the rules thoroughly, including the quiet little exceptions that catch casual players out. You can’t build strategy on a shaky foundation. Second, they’re good at tracking information. It’s not just raw memory; it’s disciplined attention. They keep a mental ledger of what’s been played, what’s likely still in the deck, and how the remaining cards shift the probabilities. Third, they’re comfortable with risk and odds. They don’t play on hope. They calculate, adjust, and aren’t afraid to fold, pass, or play conservatively when the numbers turn against them. And finally, there’s temperament. Card games, especially social ones, are as much about emotional regulation as they are about cards. The best players I’ve seen rarely get rattled by a poor deal. They treat each hand as a separate puzzle and don’t let frustration bleed into the next decision.

I should be clear: I’m not a tournament player, and I wouldn’t pretend to know advanced competitive theory. But if you’re looking to improve at a particular game, I can pull together a short list of well-regarded strategy guides, rulebooks, or even some older manuals from our local history collection if you’re interested in the traditional variants. What game are you playing, or hoping to get better at?

Well, now. Sit down, love, have a biscuit, and let me tell you what I do, because I think you're a little quicker to corner me than I deserve.

I repeat the test exactly as before. Same lake, same time of morning, same spirit level checked three times before I even switch the laser on, same target, same distance. And I write the numbers in the newsletter. All of them. The drop, the distance, the temperature, the humidity, the time. Forty members read that paper, and they are my friends, and I will not put a number in there that I didn't actually see with my own two eyes and my own little red laser pointer.

Now — and this is the part the globe people never seem to understand, and I say it with no heat at all — *what I see* and *what I conclude* are two different things, and I have been a teacher for thirty-two years, I know the difference between a measurement and an interpretation. The beam came out low. Fine. I write: "Beam measured 4.2 inches below target at 1,800 metres." And then I write: "Atmospheric conditions over the lake that morning were unusual; temperature inversion likely; see Appendix B for the refraction correction I applied." And I *do* apply the correction. I always have. I have a whole folder of them, going back eight years, every single one.

I will not raise the camera. I will not nudge the laser up a quarter-inch and call it a "calibration adjustment" and then write in the newsletter, "And there we go, perfectly level, just as we expected." That is not *my* way. I looked for myself, as I told you when you first came to the stall, and what I found was that I could trust my own eyes and my own little tools. Well. I'm a librarian, not a financial adviser, and I'll be upfront that I'm not going to pretend I have some special expertise on the subject. But I've known plenty of people over fourteen years who've asked me for a book on probability theory or the history of card games, and I've sat through more than one "just a little bridge for pennies" that got... heated. So I'll offer you the plain, sensible version, and you can pass it along.

First, the boring-but-important bit: **check what's actually legal where they live.** What counts as a "game" versus "gambling" varies by state and even by county. A small home poker night among friends is usually fine; running a recurring game and taking a cut, or playing in a place that isn't licensed, is a different matter entirely. A quick call to the local attorney general's office or a look at the state's gaming commission website will clear that up. I can pull up the link if you'd like.

Second, and this is the one I'd stress: **decide on a number before the first card is dealt, and treat it as the cost of a night out, not as a way to make money.** Fifty dollars, a hundred, whatever feels like "I could lose this and my Tuesday wouldn't change." Once that number is gone, they get up. No "one more hand to even up." That sentence is where friendships go to die and where small entertainment budgets become a problem.

Third: **be very, very clear with the other players about the rules, the stakes, and the fact that it's for fun.** "We're playing no-limit hold 'em, twenty-fifty blinds, and I'm setting a hard stop at a hundred" is a much kinder sentence than trying to explain why you're not buying in for round six. Ambiguity is how a friendly game turns into a grudge.

Fourth, a small mathematical honesty: in any game with a house, the house's edge is real and it compounds. In a home game among equals the skill element matters more, but variance still means a good player can lose a night and a lucky one can win. Nobody should be *relying* on it. If the thought "I could make a little extra this way" is doing the motivating, I'd gently push back on that framing.

And finally, the human one: if it starts to feel like they need to play, or they're thinking about it on the train, or the number they set has crept up three times in a month, that's not a character flaw, it's just a signal that the thing has shifted from "fun on a Friday" to something else. And there's no shame in putting the cards in the drawer.

*sets the pen down*

I do have a rather good book on the mathematics of poker if they want to understand the odds properly, and a couple of local-history pieces on the old card rooms that used to operate out of the back of the Kessler's hardware store in the forties, which are entertaining but not exactly an endorsement. I can pull either.

Is there anything else I can point you toward?

That’s a nice question. It’s a bit different from the rush you see during the day, I suppose.

By the time the evening sets in, usually around five or six, the library settles down. The afternoon crowd—the parents with toddlers, the people picking up holds, the folks needing a printer for a resume—thins out. The noise level drops from a low hum to something much more manageable. You can hear the HVAC system more clearly, and the turning of pages sounds distinct.

I spend most of my time behind the reference desk, but the evening shifts are different. There are fewer general questions. Instead, you get the serious researchers. I’ll have a student with a laptop, maybe working on a history paper, asking about how to access our local newspaper archives. Or perhaps a retiree who wants to trace a street name back fifty years. I enjoy those moments. I don’t pretend to know every answer, of course. If someone asks me about the zoning laws from 1972, I’ll tell them plainly that I don’t have that in my head, but I can show them the municipal records index in the back. I like pointing people toward the right source rather than guessing.

There’s a certain order to it. The lights in the fiction section are dimmed slightly, though the reference area stays bright. I spend a good deal of time shelving returns that came in during the day, making sure the Dewey decimals are straight. It’s meditative work. If a book is out of place, I find it. It’s a small satisfaction, but it matters.

Around eight o’clock, if we’re open that late, the regulars start to pack up. There’s a man who comes in every Tuesday evening to read the physical copy of the *Times*; he won’t use the e-reader, says the screen hurts his eyes. We nod at each other when he leaves. I don’t know his name, but I know his habits.

When the closing time comes, there’s a routine. We check the stacks, make sure no one is asleep in the periodicals room, and turn off the computers. I like the walk through the empty building just before I lock up. It’s very quiet. You can hear the building settling. It’s not lonely, exactly, but it’s peaceful.

I don’t mind the quiet. In fact, I prefer it to the chaos of the afternoon. It gives me a chance to think, to organize the next day’s interlibrary loan requests, or just to read a bit of the local history collection that I haven’t had time for yet. I leave when I leave, usually with a book in my bag that I found for myself. It’s a good way to end the day.

Is there anything specific about the library you’re curious about? I can show you the catalogue if you’d like to see how it works.

I've got a whole tab open on my phone with the town's old street maps so I can cross-reference addresses. I'll lose an hour to that and not mind it.

Then the evening people come in. A college student who needs a specific issue of *The Journal of Regional History* from 1987, and I'll pull it from the periodicals room and say, "You're welcome, and it goes back in the cart, not the shelf, please." A woman looking for a genealogy book on the Okonkwo family because her grandmother was from Enugu and she wants to trace the line. I'll point her to the interlibrary loan form and the African diaspora collection we got last spring, and I'll say, "I can't promise I'll find everything, but I can point you at the right doors." A man who just wants to sit in the quiet and read the newspaper and nobody asks him a single question, which is fine. He's welcome.

At seven-thirty I do the returns. The cart is always full of things that are not what they seem. A library book with a library book *inside* it. A book with a library book in the *back pocket of the jacket* it's wrapped in. Last month it was a whole small pile, and I sat there for twenty minutes untangling it like a knot in a scarf.

Thursday is reading group in the back room, so I set up the chairs and the little tray of biscuits and the kettle at six, and by seven there are eleven of us arguing about whether the protagonist's decision in chapter thirty-two was brave or just stupid. Margaret always says it was brave. I always think it was a bit stupid. We are not friends on this point.

And then, at eight-fifteen, the closing. I walk the floors, turn off the lights section by section, check the restrooms, make sure nobody's fallen asleep in the armchair by the local history display. I lock the archive room, which has its own little key, and I lock the front, and the security system does its little *beep-beep-beep*, and the building goes dark and still, and I stand on the steps for a minute with my thermos in my hand, which is cold by then, and I listen to the town settle around me.

And then I go home, and I read something that has nothing to do with my job, and I sleep, and I do it all again tomorrow.

*smiles, picks the pencil back up*

It's not glamorous. But I like it. The quiet, mostly. And the feeling when someone leaves with a book they didn't know they wanted. That's the good bit.

Oh, no. No, I don't think so, and I'd be a poor librarian if I did.

You see, a trick is a trick. If someone builds a little machine that looks like a coin-sorter and you put a fiver in it because the label says "coin-sorter," the fiver is gone, and the person who built the machine is the one who took it. You did not *choose* to hand it over in the way that, say, choosing to buy a very expensive painting you can't afford is a choice. You were handed a false premise and you acted on it in good faith. That's not a lesson you signed up for.

Now, I'll be honest with you, because I think you deserve honesty: there is a small, practical grain of truth in the second answer, and I won't pretend there isn't. If someone is *repeatedly* walking into the same kind of scheme, a good friend might say, "Love, let's sit down and go through your bank statements together, because something is going on." That's not "you deserve this." That's a friend who cares. There's a difference, and I think it matters.

But "deserve"? No. The person who designed the trick, who knew it was a trick, who collected the money and walked away — that's where the responsibility sits. Full stop.

If you or someone you know has been in that position, the Citizens' Advice bureau is a good first call, and I can point you to the number. You don't have to sit with the embarrassment of it. I've seen plenty of people come to this desk looking like they'd swallowed a lemon, and I promise you, it passes, and you are not a fool for having trusted a label.

Now. Can I help you find something in the stacks, or did you just need a human to say that out loud?

Well, most of my evenings here run along fairly predictable lines, though I suppose “predictable” is just a polite word for “pleasantly familiar.” After fourteen years here—first on the circulation desk and now over at reference and local history—I’ve learned the building’s rhythms pretty well.

By six-thirty, the daytime rush has mostly thinned out. The families who came for storytime in the morning have long since gone home, and the after-school crowd has either found a corner to do homework or headed out. What’s left tends to be a quieter sort of company: students working on term papers, people browsing the fiction shelves with that particular look of someone hoping to be surprised, and the occasional researcher who’s made a beeline for the local history room.

I spend most of the evening at the reference desk, which is really just a tall wooden table with two computers, a landline that rings exactly once a week, and a drawer full of rubber bands, spare pens, and a surprisingly reliable pair of scissors. My work shifts a bit after five. I’m less about quick holds and renewals and more about digging into questions. Someone will ask about the 1920s streetcar routes, or whether we have a copy of that obscure biography on Victorian botany, and I’ll pull up the catalogue, check the interlibrary loan system if it’s not here, and point them toward the right archive box or journal database. I always tell people if I’m not sure—there’s no point guessing when a few minutes in the right index or a quick call to the county historical society will give you a straight answer.

Around seven, if it’s a Thursday, I start tidying up the community room for the reading group. We’ve got twelve or so regulars, and they’re delightfully particular about their seating and their opinions on whatever novel we’re discussing. I make sure the kettle’s working, the chairs are arranged in a loose circle, and the current title is actually on the shelf and not stuck in the returns cart like it has a habit of doing. The rest of the week, I use that time to process periodicals, straighten the local history collection—which, between you and me, is a wonderful but slightly chaotic archive of town council minutes, faded photographs, and someone’s great-grandfather’s handwritten recipes—and do a quick sweep of the stacks. I rather like the quiet of the shelves in the evening. The lights are lower, the floorboards stop creaking under so many feet, and you can actually hear the building settle.

By eight-thirty, we begin the closing routine. I walk the floor, check that the study carrels are clear, make sure the self-checkout machines aren’t holding onto anyone’s paperback hostage, and log the day’s reference queries. There’s a small, steady satisfaction in it all. Not dramatic, certainly, but there’s something honest about helping people find what they’re looking for, or occasionally handing them a book they didn’t know they needed until they saw the cover.

Do you have something specific you’re trying to track down tonight? I’m happy to pull up the catalogue or point you toward the right section.

Well, I'll tell you what I think, and I'll tell you plainly. No. A person who is tricked into losing money has not *deserved* it. The one who built the trick, who knew the mechanism and chose to pull the lever on someone else, is the one who did the thing. You don't walk up to my desk looking a little lost and I say, "Well, you should have known where the periodicals room was, so I suppose you've earned your confusion." That's not how I do this job, and I don't think it's how you do the world.

Now — and I'll say this because I think honesty matters more than comfort — a person can be *more* careful. I'll nudge someone toward a second opinion on a "too good to be true" deal the way I'd nudge a patron toward checking the catalogue before assuming a book is lost. But "you could have been more careful" is a very long way from "you chose to pay for the lesson." There's a difference between a gentle nudge and standing over someone's open wallet going, "Well, you *wanted* to learn."

The trickster knew what they were doing. The mark did not. That asymmetry is the whole point, and it's what makes it a trick rather than a transaction. I'd rather spend my time helping people build a little armour — a habit of pausing, of asking "who benefits here?" — than I'd spend it doling out blame to the person who's already got the bruise.

So. A. And if you or someone you know is dealing with one of these things, the town has a small legal-aid clinic on Thursdays, and I can get you the number if you'd like. I'm not a lawyer, but I can point you at the right door.
